The Congress party on Friday said it favoured resolving the issue of delimitation through consultations with all political parties, but accused the government of making no effort to engage the Opposition on the matter.
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the party’s position was guided by a four-point formula: retaining the existing strength of 543 seats in the Lok Sabha; maintaining the present State-wise distribution of seats; reserving one-third (182) of the existing seats for women; and imposing a 25-year freeze on all three arrangements.
Mr. Ramesh said the need for an early consensus on the issue had become more pressing in view of of the fact that Article 82 of the Constitution will come into force and delimitation would be held once the results of the ongoing Census exercise are out early next year.
This could be unfavourable to some southern states – which have made progress in population control – and hence not feasible, he added.
Mr. Ramesh said the Congress was not opposed to delimitation as such, but believed that the exercise should not place any State at a disadvantage.
The Congress leader claimed that all parties in the INDIA bloc, including the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar), were on the same page on the four-point formula.
The DMK, he said, was also party to a resolution opposing any change in the number of Lok Sabha seats and seeking safeguards to ensure that Tamil Nadu was not disadvantaged by delimitation.
The Congress leader said seeking consultation was necessary because the government had not initiated any meaningful engagement with the Opposition.
He claimed that as per his information, the government has not shared a concrete proposal on delimitation even with constituents of the National Democratic Alliance.
The Congress wanted the matter to be discussed with all political parties and stakeholders to arrive at a consensus, Mr. Ramesh added.
The Monsoon session of Parliament has remained unprorogued since both Houses were adjourned sine die on August 13.
The decision has fuelled speculation about the possibility of the government convening Parliament at short notice to consider the proposed constitutional changes linked to women’s reservation and delimitation.
An extended or special sitting within the same session requires a minimum notice of two days, while convening a fresh session requires at least 14 days’ notice.
Speculation also continues over the timing of the winter session. Parliament has not held a winter session on four occasions: in 1975, 1979, 1984 and 2020.
